notes.meaning: Abraham's servant asks the young woman who her father is and whether her family has room for his group to stay overnight. He had just seen God answer his test at the well, but he still needed to know if she belonged to Abraham's family. His question shows how practical he was, looking for both family ties and shelter after a long journey.

Rebekah explains that her father is Bethuel, whose parents were Nahor and Milcah. This meant she was closely related to Abraham, because Nahor was Abraham's brother. The servant's search was over, since God had led him straight to Abraham's own kin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars observe that the family tree places Rebekah in the generation after Isaac rather than in his own generation.

notes.meaning: Rebekah warmly offers generous hospitality without any hesitation. She lets him know that her family has plenty of food and straw for the camels, as well as space for the travelers to sleep. Her quick generosity proved she was kind and ready to welcome strangers.

The servant instantly bows his head and falls to the ground to worship the Lord. Hearing that the young woman was Abraham's relative filled him with awe and gratitude. Before doing anything else, he stops to thank God right where he is standing.

The servant praises God for keeping His promises of loyal love and faithfulness to Abraham. He acknowledges that his success was not luck or his own doing, but the Lord guiding his steps directly to his master's family. When God answers prayer, it is right to give Him all the credit.

Rebekah rushes ahead to her family home to tell everyone what has taken place at the well. She goes straight to her mother's quarters, which were the living spaces set aside for the women in the household. Running ahead allowed her family to get ready to receive their unexpected guest.

Rebekah's brother Laban hears her report and notices the costly gold jewelry on her hands. Seeing this great wealth, he dashes out to the spring to meet the traveler standing by his camels. Laban's fast response shows the common custom of hospitality, though the rich gifts certainly caught his attention.

Laban welcomes the traveler warmly, addressing him as one blessed by the Lord. He urges him not to stay outside by the spring, since the house and the camel stalls are already prepared. Laban used the name of the Lord because Rebekah had recounted how the servant praised God at the well.

The servant and his men are brought into the house, and their camels are unloaded, fed, and bedded down with straw. Water is also brought out so the travelers can wash the dust of the road off their feet. Caring for the animals first and washing the visitors were basic duties of godly hospitality in that culture.

A meal is set before the servant, but he refuses to take a single bite until he explains why he has come. His master's business matters more to him than his own hunger or comfort after a exhausting trip. Laban listens and tells him to go ahead and speak.

The man begins by declaring that he is Abraham's servant. He does not try to pretend he is someone grand, but openly shares his identity. This immediately connects him to the household, because Abraham was a respected relative they knew well.

The servant explains that the Lord has richly blessed Abraham with immense wealth and honor. He lists Abraham's livestock, servants, silver, and gold to show that God has prospered him in every way. He is careful to point out that all this success came from God, not just human effort.

The servant tells how Abraham's wife Sarah gave birth to a son in her old age by God's special power. He adds that Abraham has given this son, Isaac, everything he owns. This showed Rebekah's family that Isaac was the sole heir of a vast household and a fitting match for marriage.

The servant recounts the solemn promise Abraham made him swear before setting out. Abraham strictly ordered him not to choose a wife for Isaac from the local Canaanites, but to travel to his own relatives instead. Abraham wanted Isaac's wife to come from a family that honored the true God rather than pagan idols.

The servant recalls the honest worry he shared with Abraham before leaving home. He had asked what would happen if the chosen woman refused to leave her family and travel back with him. It was a reasonable concern, given the long distance and life-changing choice involved.

The servant repeats Abraham's reassuring reply that the Lord would send His angel to grant success on the journey. Abraham lived a life of faithful obedience before God and fully trusted His guidance. This gave the servant confidence that God was working invisibly to prepare the way.

Abraham had assured his servant that he would be completely free from his oath if the relatives refused to let the woman go. The servant's duty was to obey faithfully and ask, but the final outcome was in God's hands. He was responsible for his obedience, not for controlling the choices of others.

The servant describes arriving at the spring that very day and praying for God's help. He had asked the God of his master Abraham to show whether his mission would succeed. He wanted everyone present to realize that what happened was an answer to prayer, not a chance meeting.

The servant explains the specific sign he had asked for while waiting by the spring. He asked that the young woman who offered a drink to him and then offered to draw water for all ten camels would be the bride God chose for Isaac. This test looked for a woman who was naturally humble, hardworking, and kind.

The servant finishes by explaining that Rebekah appeared with her water jar before he had even finished praying silently in his heart. No human being had heard his private prayer, so Rebekah could not have staged her kind actions. God proved His presence by answering the silent thoughts of his heart before he even finished asking.
